extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) evaluating novelty/anticipation under U.S. law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and responding to anticipation/novelty issues under 35 U.S.C. §102 (MPEP 2131). Focuses on when a claim is properly rejected as anticipated, what counts as prior art, enablement/inherency requirements, and strategic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Anticipation (35 U.S.C. §102 rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 35 USC 102 rejection ("anticipation rejection") occurs when the USPTO examiner determines that the invention is not novel because all elements of the claimed invention are disclosed in a single prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation is lack of novelty; it requires that every claim element is disclosed by the single prior art reference. This sets the fundamental standard for evaluating novelty rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single Reference Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim as anticipated, the disclosure must teach every element required by the claim under its broadest reasonable interpretation. Anticipation requires all elements in a claim to be found in a single piece of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner/practitioner must verify that a single reference, by itself, discloses every claim limitation (no combination of references permitted for anticipation). Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim when comparing to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements Required for Valid Anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: For a valid 102 anticipation rejection: 1) All elements of the claimed invention found in a single prior art reference; 2) Prior art must disclose the identical invention 'arranged as in the claim'; 3) Prior art reference must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three elements are required: identity of elements, arrangement as claimed, and enablement. Failure of any of these defeats an anticipation rejection. 'Arranged as in the claim' emphasizes that the prior art must disclose the claimed combination/organization, not merely isolated elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of Prior Art (Post-AIA) — §102(a)(1) and §102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application is barred if the claimed invention was: (102(a)(1)) Patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date; (102(a)(2)) Described in a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication or PCT publication that names another inventor and was filed before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between publicly-available disclosures (publications, public use, on-sale) and disclosures in earlier-filed U.S./PCT patents or publications. For §102(a)(2), pay attention to filing date of the patent/publication and named inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace Period (102(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date is not prior art if: the disclosure was made by the inventor or joint inventor, or the disclosure was made by another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For disclosures within one year of the effective filing date, determine the source of the disclosure; if tied to the inventor (or someone who derived the subject matter from the inventor), the disclosure may be excluded as prior art under the statutory grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Exceptions (102(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure under 102(a)(2) is not prior art if: it is by another who obtained the subject matter from the inventor; the subject matter was previously publicly disclosed by the inventor; or there is common ownership/joint research agreement (CREATE Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply 102(b)(2) exceptions to block earlier-filed patents/publications from being treated as prior art when there is derivation, prior inventor disclosure, or qualifying joint research/common ownership. Consider CREATE Act provisions when ownership/agreements exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency Doctrine for Anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a feature is not explicitly disclosed, it may be inherent in the prior art: it must necessarily be present (not merely possible), a skilled artisan would recognize it, and inherent disclosure is sufficient for anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat mere possibility or probability as inherency; the missing feature must necessarily flow from the prior art. Evidence and reasoning should show inevitability, and a skilled artisan would recognize the inherent feature. Inherency can establish anticipation when explicit disclosure is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement for Prior Art Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art must enable the skilled artisan to make and use the invention: mere mention without enablement is insufficient. This requirement is different from §103 (where references can be combined). Enabling reference can come from the same source or extrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a single-reference anticipation, evaluate whether the reference provides enough detail (or coupled with common knowledge/extrinsic evidence) to enable practice of the claimed invention. If the prior art does not enable, it cannot anticipate even if it mentions the elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Requirements When Asserting a 102 Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners cite the most relevant prior art reference. The rejection should identify each claim limitation, map each to specific portions of the prior art, and be specific about where each element is disclosed (column/line, paragraph, figure number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper 102 rejections must be specific and show clear mappings from claim limitations to particular disclosure locations in the reference. Vague citations or failure to identify where limitations are disclosed is a defect in the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic Responses to a 102 Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal responses include: 1) Argue claim language distinguishing from prior art; 2) Argue absence of element (not all elements disclosed); 3) Argue lack of enablement (reference doesn't enable practice); 4) Antedate the reference (swear behind under pre-AIA); 5) Invoke grace period (post-AIA inventor disclosures); 6) Amend claims to add limitations not in prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select responses based on factual record: parse claim interpretation arguments, identify missing elements or enablement defects, rely on statutory grace/antedating where available, or amend claims to recite features absent from the cited reference. Use evidence (declarations, dates, publications) to support arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA vs Post-AIA Differences Relevant to Anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA operated under a first-to-invent system (effective for applications filed before March 16, 2013); Post-AIA uses first-inventor-to-file (March 16, 2013 forward). Pre-AIA included subsections (a)-(g); Post-AIA simplified to (a) and (b) with grace period exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine application filing regime (pre- vs post-AIA) to know which statutory provisions and procedures apply (e.g., antedating/swearing behind available pre-AIA). The applicable regime affects available defenses and how prior art is characterized.
